source.title: Showing SAE Latents Are Not Atomic Using Meta-SAEs

record.tranche_reason: The post presents meta-SAE decompositions and targeted interventions as evidence that ordinary SAE latents need not be atomic, refining the claim about SAE dictionary features rather than testing the original toy-model superposition setup.
record.gate_note: The post's results on decomposing SAE decoder directions, comparing latent relationships, and steering city attributes bear on V5. References to toy-model feature composition and prior work are not results of this post. The post does not test the claim's sparse-feature geometry, capacity competition, or whether LLM features are distributed across neurons.
record.test_reason: The post decomposes GPT2-small layer-8 SAE decoder directions with a meta-SAE. It finds sparse, interpretable sub-components and uses them for targeted causal edits. It argues from these results that SAE latents are not atomic or canonical units, which bears directly on V5. It does not run toy models, test capacity accounts, measure neuron-level distribution, or test feature dimensionality.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that SAE latents are likely common compositions of more basic units rather than atomic units. Meta-SAEs give a lossy, possibly 'more atomic' but not maximally atomic decomposition that enables finer edits. They do not claim to have found true atoms.
record.recipe_differences: The post trains an SAE on the decoder directions of another SAE, rather than using the original toy-model superposition setup. It also compares meta-SAE decompositions with smaller SAEs and uses meta-latents for causal steering.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that relationships differ between meta-latents and smaller SAE latents; the meta-SAE trained on multiple SAE sizes assigns fewer active meta-latents on average to latents in smaller SAEs. Some city-attribute combinations can be edited and others cannot.
record.code_released: not stated; the post links to meta-SAE and SAE weights and a feature-explorer dashboard.
record.problems: The authors state that the work studies a single meta-SAE, a single SAE, one layer of one small model, and only a small number of city pairs. The meta-SAE decomposition is lossy; the authors lack a complete understanding of how the data distribution, SAE latents, and meta-latents relate. They describe the steering study as simplified and informal and note that more validation is needed. Some comparisons are presented only in plots, and the post reports no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: No reported claim-relevant result rows were left out.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep or geometry analysis.
No test of capacity competition or feature importance.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
No measurement of neuron-level distribution or of SAE recovery against ground truth.
Completeness and cross-seed or cross-method stability are not tested. Only one model (GPT2-small), one layer, one meta-SAE and three cities were used.

missing.what: Einstein latent decomposition and comparison table: meta-latents vs top-cosine SAE-49152 and SAE-3072 latents, with cosine values. SAE-3072 gives a similar decomposition, implying the units depend on dictionary size.
missing.locator: Meta-latents form interpretable decompositions; Are Meta-Latents different from SAE Latents? (Einstein table)

missing.what: Latents in smaller SAEs activate fewer meta-latents on average (figure on meta-latent counts by SAE size).
missing.locator: Using Meta-SAEs to Interpret Split Features, final figure

missing.what: Reconstruction comparison including the random-direction decoder baseline (figure, no numbers in text).
missing.locator: Are Meta-Latents different from SAE Latents? reconstruction variants

record.verdict_notes: The reader's limits_scope label rested on untested scope (a single model), which belongs under untested parts, so it was dropped. The control rows R5-R8 duplicate baselines. Steering is informal: only logprobs on single-token attributes were measured, with no general-performance check. The authors concede smaller-SAE decompositions may give similar results.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, sparsity sweep, or test of overlapping nearly orthogonal directions or regular geometry.
No test of neuron polysemanticity as a consequence of competition for limited capacity or of feature importance determining dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of alternative causes of polysemantic neurons.
The post does not measure feature distribution across neurons or assess SAE recovery of sparse features against an independent reference.
Tests decompositions and some causal edits for GPT2-small layer 8, but not completeness, stability, or canonicity across models, layers, training conditions, or SAE methods.
Does not test whether the underlying network features are one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: GPT2-small
rows.operation_detail: Compared meta-latent decompositions of SAE decoder directions across SAE sizes.

conditions.value: 768 to 98304; one meta-SAE trained on 8 SAEs
talk latent in SAE size 24576 and its split in size 49152

rows.measure: Number and composition of active meta-latents for the broad latent and its split latents
rows.baseline: SAE size 24576 latent 8326 had one active meta-latent, 589.
rows.value: In SAE size 49152, the latent splits into seven more specific latents; the examples listed have meta-latent 589 and some have additional meta-latents.
rows.locator: Using Meta-SAEs to Interpret Split Features
rows.note: The post says the broader latent splits by adding meta-latents; this is evidence against treating the larger SAE latents as necessarily atomic.
rows.check: Relative to V5 the state is reversed, not observed. A broad 'talk' latent (one meta-latent, 589) splits into seven larger-SAE latents that add further meta-latents. So latents are composite and depend on dictionary size. This used a separate meta-SAE trained on 8 SAEs.

source_check.locator_found: Using Meta-SAEs to Interpret Split Features, lines 205–243.

rows.subject: GPT2-small
rows.operation_detail: Compared reconstruction using original meta-SAE decoder directions with variants using SAE decoder directions.

conditions.value: replace meta-SAE decoder directions with maximum-cosine SAE directions from SAEs sized 768 to 6144, then fine-tune encoder for 5000 epochs

rows.value: Reconstruction using the SAE decoder directions and fine-tuned encoder was only slightly worse than using the original meta-SAE.
rows.locator: Are Meta-Latents different from SAE Latents?
rows.note: The post gives no numerical reconstruction values.
rows.check: This compares the meta-SAE method with baselines built from smaller-SAE directions, and there is also a random-direction baseline. No numbers are given. It mainly shows smaller SAEs can serve as decomposition bases, an indirect point on canonicity.

rows.subject: GPT2-small
rows.operation_detail: Compared SAE-49k adjacency graphs built from shared meta-latents and from shared cosine-similar SAE-3k latents.

conditions.value: Both graphs set to contain the same number of edges

rows.locator: Are Meta-Latents different from SAE Latents?
rows.note: The text describes this as evidence that the meta-SAE captures substantially different latent relationships; its wording refers to a ratio of shared edges and then says vertices.
rows.check: This compares methods (meta-SAE graph vs cosine graph). The text mixes up 'shared edges' and 'vertices' for the 28.92% figure, and the baseline is a different method rather than a control for V5.

rows.subject: GPT2-small
rows.operation_detail: Compared maximum cosine similarities among meta-SAE latents and SAE latents.
rows.measure: Distribution of maximum cosine similarities and availability of a similar SAE latent
rows.value: Meta-SAE latents are generally more orthogonal than SAE-49152 latents, but the post says this difference is explained by dictionary size because SAE-3072 has a similar distribution. Many meta-latents lack an SAE-49152 latent with cosine similarity greater than 0.7, while they often have one in SAE-3072.
rows.locator: Are Meta-Latents different from SAE Latents?
rows.note: The post describes the plots but supplies no plotted values beyond the cosine threshold.
rows.check: The cosine-similarity distributions are figure-only, with no values beyond the 0.7 threshold. This is a method comparison, not a direct measure of SAE-latent atomicity.

rows.subject: GPT2-small

rows.measure: Whether country, language, continent, and currency edits were achieved
rows.value: Reported successful patterns include currency only; language plus currency; country, language, and currency; and country, language, continent, and currency. The post says not all combinations could be edited.
rows.locator: Causally Intervening and Making Targeted Edits with Meta-Latents
rows.note: The table is flattened in the text; each row lists combinations of attributes and the associated meta-latents. A fully successful four-attribute edit is reported, but some combinations fail.
rows.check: Only 4 non-trivial attribute combinations out of the enumerated set could be edited, so decomposability into separately editable parts is incomplete. The table is flattened.

source_check.correct: State relative to V5: reversed. Reported nontrivial edit patterns are currency only; language and currency; country, language and currency; all four attributes. Not every attribute combination is achievable.

source_check.problem: Partial describes the method's attribute-editing coverage, rather than partial occurrence of V5; the selective edits provide evidence against atomic dictionary units.

relationships.condition: GPT2-small layer-8 residual SAEs (49k and multi-size) with a BatchTopK meta-SAE, and the Tokyo→Paris attribute edit
relationships.reason: SAE latents decompose into interpretable meta-latents and split across sizes by adding them (R1). Meta-latent edits change language and currency while keeping country and continent (R13-R16). Both indicate SAE latents are composite, not atomic units. Some combinations fail (R17).
relationships.display_finding: SAE latents broke down into interpretable meta-latents, and adding meta-latents reproduced how latents split across SAE sizes. In the Tokyo-to-Paris edit, changing meta-latents shifted language and currency while country and continent stayed fixed, though some combinations failed.

labels.reason: R1 documents compositional splitting across SAE sizes; R13–R16 jointly show language and currency changing while country and continent preferences remain. These challenge atomic-unit interpretations. R17 limits editing flexibility without establishing atomicity.

relation.reason: Its own GPT2-small experiments bear on whether SAE dictionary latents are fundamental representational units.

tranche.reason: The post presents decompositions and selective causal edits as evidence against treating SAE latents as atomic units, directly questioning V5.

source_check.notes: The authors' conclusion is accurately paraphrased: decompositions are lossy and meta-latents are not guaranteed true atoms. The splitting experiment uses a separate multi-size meta-SAE; its text states seven split latents but lists six examples. Completeness and seed stability are untested.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: GPT2-small layer 8 SAE decompositions and the Tokyo-to-Paris steering task
reader_labels.reason: A broad SAE latent decomposes into multiple meta-latents and targeted meta-latent edits can change selected city attributes while preserving others, challenging the claim that SAE features are complete, canonical units (R1, R13-R17).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: The post's tested model and meta-SAE setup
reader_labels.reason: The evidence comes from a single small model and a limited steering case study; the decompositions are lossy and the authors do not claim that meta-latents are true or maximally atomic units (R1, R13-R17).
